# Introduction

The incidence of diabetes has increased significantly in recent decades with an age-standardized rate of 234/100,000 in 1990 to 285/100,000 people in 2017 [@liuTrendsIncidenceDiabetes2020].
According to estimates by the International Diabetes Federation, the number of people with diabetes is projected to increase to 52 million by 2050 in South and Central America [@internationaldiabetesfederationIDFDiabetesAtlas2021]. 
Findings from a Peruvian study showed a cumulative incidence of diabetes of 7.2% and an incidence rate of 19.5 (95% CI 13.9 to 28.3) new cases per 1,000 person-years. These results indicate that the incidence of diabetes in Peru is among the highest reported worldwide [@seclenElevatedIncidenceRates2017] (7). Although, reports on the incidence of diabetes in Peru remain limited and the few number of studies has been performed in urban populations.
The objective of this study is to estimate  age,  sex, and age-standardized incidence rates of diabetes in Peru for the calendar years 2018 to 2023 by implementing the illness-death model.

# Methods
An observational study will be carried out with cross-sectional data from the Demographic and Family Health Surveys (ENDES) from 2018 to 2023. Based on these surveys, the prevalent cases of DM at the national level in Peru will be identified. The ENDES survey is carried out annually and is representative of the entire territory of Peru, which generates information on demographic dynamics, health status of mothers and children under 5 years of age, communicable diseases and non-communicable diseases, among other aspects. The target population consists of households and their respective resident members, in which data is collected by trained personnel who visit the selected households. The instruments for collecting information vary from interviews to laboratory measurements [@EncuestaDemograficaSalud].
To identify the prevalent cases of diabetes from the ENDES survey, the question will be used as an indicator: Has a doctor ever diagnosed you with diabetes or "high sugar" in your blood? This question presents the following answer options: yes, no, don't know/don't remember [@EncuestaDemograficaSalud]. For the analyses, only participants who have answered with the options "yes" or "no" will be included, excluding those whose answer has been "do not know/do not remember".
Subsequently, the age-specific prevalence of diabetes will be estimated by age and sex for the years 2015 to 2023. The age groups will be categorized into five-year periods from 15-19 years to 90-95 years with their respective 95% confidence interval using the method of log-transformed intervals. Additionally, data from the United Nations World Population Prospects will be used to obtain the mortality rate in the general population for the years 2015 to 2023. For estimating incidence using the approach described below, information on the mortality rate ratio (MRR) for people with vs. without diabetes is needed. Since no studies estimated the MRR for Peru so far, we will model several scenarios and vary the MRR within a plausible range, as was done in previous studies [@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024]. Both the data from the ENDES survey and the United Nations World Population Prospects are freely accessible.
To estimate the incidence rate of diabetes for the years 2018 to 2023, an illness-death model will be applied using a partial differential equation. This method has previously been used in the context of chronic non-communicable diseases [@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014; @hassAgespecificIncidenceNeed2023]. This model is based on a mathematical relationship between the prevalence of diabetes, the mortality rate in the general population, and the MRR. The transition between these states is characterized by the incidence rates (no diabetes → diabetes) and mortality rates rates (no diabetes → death; diabetes → death).

The partial differential equation used to estimate the incidence of DM was developed by Brinks and Landwehr [@brinksAgeTimedependentModel2014] and describes the change in prevalence with respect to age and calendar time:

$$
i = \frac{\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial a} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right)p}{1 - p} + m \cdot \frac{p (MRR - 1)}{p (MRR - 1) + 1}
$$ {#eq-PDE}

Where $i$ represents the incidence of DM, $p$ represents the prevalence of DM, $\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial a} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right)p$ indicates the temporal change in the prevalence of DM as a function of age $a$ and calendar time $t$. Additionally, $m$ reflects the mortality rate of the general population and $MRR$ the mortality rate ratio. Therefore, the incidence rate can be calculated from estimates for the prevalence of DM, its temporal change according to age and calendar time, the overall mortality rate, and the ratio of mortality rates between people with and without DM.
All statistical analyses will be performed in the R software version 4.5.0 [@rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2023].

# Discussion
It is essential to understand the epidemiological profile of diabetes in the Peruvian population to take public health actions towards prevention and control of diabetes [@internationaldiabetesfederationHowRegistriesCan2024].
There is a lack of cohort studies conducted in Latin American countries, therefore it is not feasible to directly estimate  the incidence of diabetes. For this reason, this study will apply the illness-death model to estimate the incidence of diabetes, using prevalence data from nationally representative surveys and mortality data from official vital statistics. This model has been previously implemented using Mexican data to calculate incidence rates of diabetes in Mexico for the periods 2003-2015 [@silverman-retanaUsingIllnessdeathModel2024].
This study has some limitations. Diabetes definition is defined by self-report and therefore may introduce information bias. It is not possible to distinguish between type 1 and type 2 diabetes, which is important given the increase in the incidence of type 1 diabetes that has been reported in recent years [@gregoryGlobalIncidencePrevalence2022]. 
The strength of this study is the use of nationally representative survey data from Peru. Therefore we will contribute with recent estimates on the incidence of diabetes in Peru that has.
